newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: REUTERS POLL - ANALYSTS ON CZECH STIMULUS PLAN.
newsitem.headline: REUTERS POLL - ANALYSTS ON CZECH STIMULUS PLAN.

text.p: The Czech government is due to
announce an economic stimulus package on Wednesday aiming to
cut growing budget and trade deficits, accelerate economic
growth, and address problems in economic reforms.
Reuters polled a group of economists, traders and analysts
who focus on the Czech market, asking them two questions:
1. What do you think the government SHOULD do to improve
the Czech economic situation in their package of measures to be
announced on April 16?
2. What do you think the government WILL do to improve the
Czech economic situation in their package of measures to be
announced on April 16?
Their answers were
(including justifications, where given:)
Boris Gomez/Susanne Hallergard
Economic analysts, ING Barings, Prague/London
1. - Significiant cuts in speding to create budget surplus in
1997, at least Kc 20-30bn in total.
- Restraining wage growth
- freeze public sector wages at current levels for a year
- pressure management in those companies where government
has significiant holding to limit wage growth at eight to 10
percent in 1997.
- Accelerated price deregulation
- fully liberalise energy prices by start of 1999
- lift state rent controls by mid-1999
- Accelerated privatisation
- complete privatisation of IPB and one other major bank
by end of 1997
- final decision on method of privatisation of energy
distribution companies, in order to offer some assets in
second-half 1997
- timetable for selling off holdings in strategic firms
- Capital markets reforms
- introduce SEC-like agency by July 1, with international
experts on executive board
- stricter company reporting requirements (starting in
1998 all companies listed on Prague Stock Exchange's two main
markets must publish quarterly results).
- abolition of trading at Centre for Securities
(effective July 1)
- separation of banks from investment funds (legislation
effective July 1)
- Enterpreneurial sector
- Accelerated write-offs for capital equipment (from
start of 1998)
- Stricter legislation to speed up bankruptcies
- Savings
- Increase state subsidies for building societies (to
finance long-term housing loans and attract higher
contributions to saving accounts)
- Issue state bonds for domestic household savers
- Complete proposal for pension system reform by end of
1997 and approve legislation by Sept.1. Changes (including
private contribution scheme) could be phased at start of 1999
2. - Very Likely
- Significiant budget cuts, arround 20 billion crowns
- Pro-export policies (reaffirming previous promises to
widen scope of EGAP's activities; increased funds for export
bank, etc.)
- Wage growht in public sector slowed to target of 5-8
percent for 1997
- Wage growth in companies where government has influence
slowed to target of 1997
- Commitment to complete legislative proposal to reform
pension system by end of 1997
- Commitment to speed up court/bankruptcy process
- Also Likely
- "seasonal" import duties on selected foodstuffs and
more stringent non-tariff trade barriers on imports,
particulary from EU. Anti-dumping legislation to be implemented
by July 1.
- more state support for building societies (to finance
long-term loans and attract higher contributions to saving
accounts)
- commitment to improvefinancial situation of corporate
sector (shorte depreciation rules, accelerated tax write-offs
for capital equipment, etc.)
- speedier privatisation (with annoucment of timetable for
selling off assets in banks, energy distribution companies and
other strategic holdings)
- commitment to increase transparency of capital markets
(including more concrete details on setting up the SEC body in
second half 1997)
- commitment to introduce legislation to separate banks
from investment funds
- Possible
- importquotas on selected items
- state bond issue aimed at individual investors
- lowering tax on capital gains and interest
- Unlikely
- import surcharge (indecision on which items to cover,
wary of conflict with WTO and lack of consensus within cabinet)
Kamil Janacek
Chief Economist, Komercni Banka Prague
1. - run a surplus budget of about 2 to 3 percent of GDP
- quickly introduce pro-export policies
- (take) steps to improve enforcement of (economic) law
- accomplish the remaining privatisation, including big
banks and industrial corporations
2. - make cuts in public budgets keeping them in balance
- (take) steps to reduce imports of highly subsidised
agriculture and luxury goods
- issue longer-term government bonds aiming to increase the
propensity to save in the household sector
- (make) changes in legal and institutional framework
enabling better functioning of the legal infrastructure
- (make) a step-by-step finalisation of privatisation
ANDREW KENNINGHAM
Senior Economist Emerging Markets, Merrill Lynch London
1. a) announce fiscal cuts of 40-50 billion crowns, of which
30 billion to be savings in 1997 and a major part of savings to
be from reduced public sector wage increases
b) widen the exchange rate (fluctuation) band to plus/minus
10 percent but keep the mid-point the same and confirm the
commitment not to devalue;
c) announce target for reduction in the share of government
expenditure in GDP over next the 2-3 years
d) leave interest rates unchanged
Reasons:
a) monetary policy appears to be having an effect, as seen
by reduced M2 and slowing investment growth. Problem of excess
domestic demand is increasingly due to excessive growth of
consumption and real wages (as seen by Q4 GDP figures, for
example) and the budget gap. This suggests the burden should be
moved to fiscal from monetary policy. At least 25 billion
crowns of cuts are needed to give good chance of balanced
budget. Anything short of a balanced budget lacks
credibility... because of (the government's) tradition of
balance and because (the current account deficit) is heading
for 12 percent of GDP
b) a wider exchange rate band would be an indication from
the CNB that it is aware of the need for some flexibilty over
coming 12 months in the event that the current account deficit
does not decline and/or the government doesn't take tough
enough measures on the fiscal side
c) government spending/GDP is too high at around 50
percent - it should aim at below 40 percent. Particularly since
unemployment so low, this is an achievable target
d) evidence of slowdown is clear but the strength of the
slowdown not yet clear, therefore no need to relax monetary
policy too much at this stage
2. (Not provided)
MARTIN KUPKA
Economist, Patria Finance, Prague
1. - Cut budget expenditures by as much as possible. However,
too strong wage growth cuts in the public sector will
accelerate the exodus of excellent public employees to the
private sector and saving on investment will damage the future
growth. The volume of reasonable expenditure cuts is not
unlimited
- Raise the cost of consumption, first of all of
consumption of imported consumer goods
- The extra proceeds from the measure can be either used as
a complementary revenue for the sate budget or be frozen in the
CNB
- Bring the protection of the domestic market at a level
comparable with that established in countries of our trading
partners
- In an accord with the CNB, introduce a crawling band
regime for koruna.
- Establish an independent and high-powered (Securities and
Exchange Commission)
- Accelerate privatization of the remaining state stakes in
Czech companies. Special attention is to be paid to the
privatization of the largest Czech banks, where no haste can be
recommended but a constant effort to complete the process is a
must
- Raise Chinese walls between invetment banking and
commercial banking in the domestic banking sector
- Improve the quality and accelerate the speed of work of
the commercial courts
- Strengthen capacities determined to identify,
investigate, and prosecute the economic crime
- Strengthen the position of creditors versus that of
debtors, to make bankruptcies less lengthy and more efficient
- adopt measures promoting higher domestic savings
2. - Make considerable budget expenditure cuts
- (Install) pro-export and anti-import administrative
measures
- (Raise) consumption taxes
- (Create) better regulation of the capital market
- Lower administrative barriers to business, including the
acceleration of court procedures
- Change legislation to implement the other measures
suggested above, except for the crawling-band regime, which I
do not expect to be part of the package
Josef Poeschl
Economist
Vienna Institute for Comparative Economic Studies
1. - Interest rates should be kept below the level in previous
months; this would impact GDP growth positively and the
exchange rate negatively.
- The exchange rate should be allowed to decrease towards
the lower limit of the (fluctuation) band or even somewhat
below it.
- Within the limits set by international agreements,
tariffs and non-tariff barriers should restrict imports - for a
defined period of time, including plans for a gradual removal.
These barriers should differ between product categories.
- For a limited period of time, some luxory goods (e.g.
expensive cars) should be taxed additionally.
- More export promotion should be designed in such a way
that it will ease the export of final goods and more
sophisticated products.
- Taxation efficiency should be increased. For a positive
long-term development an improvement of the administrative and
judicial system will be crucial. A solution should be found for
old debt, financial relations and the capital market. Big banks
should be privatized provided that strong western partners get
involved
2. I doubt whether the goverment will introduce far-reaching
measures. Elements of the package might be an attempt to
stimulate private savings and a reduction of profit taxation.
Some non-tariff barriers will be introduced in the way Mr.
(Industry and Trade Minister Vladimir) Dlouhy suggested it.
There will be an announcement of more privatisation,
de-regulation and capital market transparency.
PAVEL SOBISEK
Chief analyst, Zivnostenska Banka, Prague
I have confidence that the government will evaluate the
situation properly and that the package will include all the
measures necessary for returning the economic development back
on the track. Therefore, I am not dividing my answer into
"should" and "will" part. The most likely scenario:
The package will be oriented on regaining balance in the
economy by adopting reductions on the demand side. An
administrative devaluation is out of the discussion.
An imports surcharge will not be imlemented due to the
subsequent distortion of the market environment as well as the
difficult feasibility of the measure.
Interest rates will be kept intact for the moment, and
their cautious decline will be allowed only in the second half
Household demand will be reduced by a combination of limits
on wage growth and incentives for long-term savings.
Government spending cuts will be included in the package,
their range will however be lower than the maximum of five
percent of the budget.
Together with continued monetary restriction, this will
support investors' confidence in the koruna (crown) and its
exchange rate will not decline dramatically for the moment. At
the same time, a strong koruna will maintain pressure on the
corporate sphere to accelerate restructuring, the result being
fast growth of the unemployment rate.
GDP growth will temporarily slow down, but may rebound
again by the end of 1997 as a result of an improved efficiency
in the economy, accompanied by better protection of domestic
market by a system of quotas and tariffs.
The main threat to success of the plan may be potential
social unrest. With the coalition currently having only a tight
majority in the parliament, and the opposition hardly expected
to collaborate in any important issue, a danger exists that the
measures could be wrecked by early parliamentary elections.
MIROSLAV SOUCEK
Chief Economist, IPB Bank, Prague
1. - Restore the budget balance (short-term task)
- Prevent a further worsening in the trade balance and
consequently in the current account balance, but without a
devaluation (long-term task)
- Acknowledge the anti-inflationary process and maintaining
of tight monetary policy as a whole (steady task)
2. - They don't consider the number of some items or details
in the package the most important. I would like to expect the
government will declare their resolution to enter into the
economy in a role of strong authority. This will help in the
necessary restoration of public confidence -- it would be the
chief precondition of success in any measures. Therefore the
most important (element) is an ability to implement the
decisions not a simple schedule of targets and remedies
MATT STARR
Bond trader, Creditanstalt Prague
1. Cap waages, (make) budget cuts, separate funds from banks,
(provide) more funds for the Export Guarantee and Insurance
agency (EGAP) and Exportni Banka, improve the speed of
bankruptcy procedures, and propose legislation to fight
financial corruption
2. Same as above
-- Prague Newsroom, 420-2-2423-0003
